title: Direct Edit, Targeted Regen, Full Restart: Which Claude Design Move to Make
excerpt: Claude Design has three iteration modes with different costs and consistency risks — reaching for full regen when a slider works wastes both.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**Claude Design has three iteration modes with different costs and consistency risks — reaching for full regen when a slider works wastes both.**

When something's wrong in a generated screen, the instinct is to re-prompt. That's often the wrong move — not just for tokens, but because each full regeneration means every previous design decision can shift.

**Three modes, ordered from cheapest to most disruptive:**

**1. Direct editing** — inline text editing, property sliders (spacing, color, radius), and element manipulation — costs nothing and consumes no tokens. Use this for cosmetic fixes: wrong label, off-brand color, too much padding. The change applies to the selected element; everything else stays.

**2. Targeted element regeneration** — select a component and prompt Claude Design to rework it alone. Use this when a component's *structure* is wrong but the rest of the screen is right: the nav uses the wrong pattern, the card layout doesn't match your system. Targeted regen keeps the page as the anchor and regenerates only the selected piece.

**3. Full page regeneration** — re-prompting the whole screen. Reserve this for when the page's layout *premise* is wrong: wrong column count, wrong hierarchy, wrong primary action placement. Everything you've already refined goes with it.

**The decision:**
- Something looks off, structure is right → direct edit (slider or inline)
- One component is the wrong shape → targeted element regen
- The page doesn't do what a user needs → full regen

The common failure is using targeted or full regen for problems a slider would fix. Those trigger generation — and generation means your previous decisions can drift. Sliders don't.

**Limit**: direct editing works on what's already generated. For a fundamentally different approach, regeneration is the only path — but arrive there only after ruling out the cheaper modes.

**Sources:** [Claude Design review, iteration modes — Salesdorado](https://salesdorado.com/en/ai/review-claude-design/) · [Claude Design workflow — designproject.io](https://designproject.io/blog/claude-design-workflow/) · [Claude for designers in 2026 — artofstyleframe.com](https://artofstyleframe.com/blog/claude-for-designers-2026/)

title: Fable 5.1 Calls Your Agent's Tools One at a Time — Fix It With One Sentence
excerpt: In Fable 5.1 coding agents, implied-independent calls may serialize. A one-sentence turn-scoped message appended after each tool batch restores parallel execution.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**In Fable 5.1 coding agents, implied-independent calls may serialize instead of batching. A one-sentence turn-scoped system message appended after each tool batch restores parallel execution.**

Fable 5.1 batches tool calls reliably when your request names what to fetch. The exception is coding agents and bash-and-editor harnesses where the next reads are *implied* by the task — there it may issue them one per turn instead of together. No quality loss, but each extra turn costs tokens, a round trip, and wall-clock time in a loop that can run dozens of turns.

**The fix:** append this sentence after each tool-result batch:

```
First privately list what you need next; then request every item that doesn't depend on another's result in this one response.
```

Deliver it as a turn-scoped system message — a `role: "system"` entry with `clear_at: "next_user_message"` (beta header: `mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21`). Append a fresh copy after each tool-result batch; leave old copies in the array byte-for-byte. Once cleared, they cost zero input tokens and the model doesn't see them. **Do not edit or delete them**: that restarts the prompt cache from that point and invalidates the thinking blocks that follow.

Without the beta flag, place the sentence in a `text` block inside the user message that carries the `tool_result` blocks — same turn, after the results.

**This is different from `disable_parallel_tool_use`**, which intentionally forces one call per turn for pipelines that need to inspect or rate-limit each result. The nudge is for loops where calls are structurally independent but the model isn't batching them on its own.

**Limit**: the nudge works for implied-independent calls in agentic loops. Calls with genuine ordering dependencies — where each result determines the next call — can't be parallelized regardless of the prompt.

**Sources:** [Batch independent tool calls — Anthropic Fable 5.1 prompting guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5-1#batch-independent-tool-calls-in-agent-loops) · [Prompting Claude Fable 5.1 (full guide) — Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5-1) · [Three Fable 5.1 patterns that break existing agents — AI Unfiltered](https://www.arturmarkus.com/anthropic-cuts-fable-5-1-cache-reads-75-to-0-25-m-and-breaks-three-prompt-patterns-developers-rely-on/)

title: Give Claude Design a Brand Brief Before Screen One — Here's What to Include
excerpt: Claude Design's default output is competent but generic. Front-loading component names, color roles, type scale, and negatives into your project description prevents the generation-by-generation ae…
author: Chris Harper
content:
**Claude Design's default output is competent but generic. Front-loading component names, color roles, type scale, and explicit negatives into your project description prevents the generation-by-generation aesthetic fight.**

When you open a new Claude Design project and write "SaaS dashboard" as your prompt, you get a SaaS dashboard — with the right sections, the right density, and buttons that look like nobody on your team approved them. The fix, "make it look more like our product," costs 3–5 correction rounds per screen and still doesn't converge, because each regeneration starts fresh from Claude's generic defaults ([Claude Design workflow — The Design Project](https://designproject.io/blog/claude-design-workflow/)).

The upstream fix is a project description that seeds every generation with your system. Practitioners report that Claude Design's project description persists as background context across generations — what you put there shapes every screen, not just the first.

**What to include (10–15 lines is enough):**

```
Component conventions:
- Buttons: filled/outlined/text variant pattern. Filled: #3B82F6 bg, white text.
- Cards: 8px radius. No drop shadow. 1px border #E2E8F0.
- Inputs: 40px height. 1px border, #3B82F6 on focus. Label above.

Color roles:
- Primary: #3B82F6. Surface: #1E293B. Text: #F1F5F9.
- No additional colors. No gradients.

Type scale: headings 24/20/16px. Body 14px. Never under 12px.

Layout: 1280px max width. 12-column grid, 24px gutter.

Negatives: no decorative illustrations. No rounded avatars with initials placeholders.
No glassmorphism. No drop shadows on non-card elements.
```

The negatives matter as much as the positives. Without them, Claude Design fills unspecified gaps with visually consistent defaults that look fine in isolation but fight your system the moment they appear next to real components.

**Sequencing with other techniques:** This project description sets stylistic consistency. It does not make Claude Design component-aware — generated screens will still use generic `<div class="btn-primary">` rather than your `<Button variant="primary">`. For component-name accuracy across screens, pair this with the component inventory step (post [2026-09-04-04](/ai-news/2026-09-04-04-claude-design-multi-screen-component-inventory)) and the substitution pass (post [2026-09-04-05](/ai-news/2026-09-04-05-claude-design-generic-to-component-substitution)). The project description reduces aesthetic drift; the inventory and substitution steps handle component accuracy.

**The limit:** A project description is static context — it doesn't update when your design system evolves. Treat it like a constraint file: review and update it whenever you change your token values or component API. Stale constraints produce subtly wrong output, and because the description isn't visible in each prompt, the drift is harder to diagnose.

**Sources:** [Claude Design workflow — The Design Project](https://designproject.io/blog/claude-design-workflow/) · [From Weeks to Hours: Claude Design Compresses Product Discovery — Product Compass](https://www.productcompass.pm/p/claude-design-product-discovery) · [Using Claude Design for prototypes and UX — Claude Academy](https://academy.claude.com/tutorials/using-claude-design-for-prototypes-and-ux)

title: Your MCP Server Is Already a LangChain Tool: Wire It Into a LangGraph Agent With MCPAdapter
excerpt: LangChain 1.4.0 alpha ships MCPAdapter — wrap any MCP server URL or local script as a LangGraph agent tool in five lines, with cached tool discovery and multi-server support via MCPClientGroup.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**LangChain 1.4.0 alpha ships `langchain.mcp.MCPAdapter` — drop in any MCP server URL or local script and your LangGraph agent discovers and calls its tools without a custom wrapper.**

The MCP-to-LangChain gap previously required either a bespoke integration or a separate client library with its own connection management. LangChain 1.4.0-alpha.3 ships a new `langchain.mcp` namespace that handles connection, tool discovery, and schema translation automatically ([LangChain release notes — Releasebot](https://releasebot.io/updates/langchain-ai)).

```python
from langchain.mcp import MCPAdapter
from langgraph.prebuilt import create_react_agent

# Accepts a URL, a local script path, an in-process server, or an MCPConfig
adapter = MCPAdapter("http://localhost:8080/mcp")
tools = await adapter.list_tools()   # discovers + adapts all server tools

agent = create_react_agent("claude-sonnet-5", tools)
result = await agent.ainvoke({"messages": [("user", "your query here")]})
```

Tool discovery is cached by default — `await adapter.list_tools(refresh=True)` repopulates it if a server changes without restarting your process.

For a fleet of servers, `MCPClientGroup` aggregates them behind one client:

```python
from langchain.mcp import MCPClientGroup

group = MCPClientGroup({
    "db":     "http://localhost:8080/mcp",
    "search": "http://localhost:8090/mcp",
})
all_tools = await group.list_tools()   # one list from all servers
agent = create_react_agent("claude-sonnet-5", all_tools)
```

This is particularly useful when you have multiple Claude Code MCP servers — the file-access server, the internal-API server, the DB query server — and want to combine them inside a LangGraph agent without writing a custom fan-out layer.

**Two limits to know upfront:**

1. **This is 1.4.0-alpha.** The `langchain.mcp` interface will shift before the final release. Pin the exact alpha version in your lockfile and watch the [LangChain releases](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/releases) before upgrading. Don't build production dependencies on an alpha API.

2. **stdio servers need an HTTP wrapper.** `MCPAdapter` expects a network endpoint (HTTP/SSE). If your MCP server runs as a local subprocess (stdio transport), you need to expose it over HTTP first — a small FastAPI wrapper around your stdio session is the standard pattern, and Claude Code's own managed MCP servers already enforce this for the same reason.

**Sources:** [LangChain 1.4.0 release notes — Releasebot](https://releasebot.io/updates/langchain-ai) · [LangChain MCPAdapter complete guide — Latenode](https://latenode.com/blog/ai-frameworks-technical-infrastructure/langchain-setup-tools-agents-memory/langchain-mcp-integration-complete-guide-to-mcp-adapters) · [MCP vs LangChain Tools — getknit.dev](https://www.getknit.dev/blog/integrating-mcp-with-popular-frameworks-langchain-openagents)

title: After Claude Design, Before Claude Code: Replace Generic HTML With Your Real Components in One Pass
excerpt: Claude Design outputs generic HTML. Before handing it to Claude Code, run one substitution pass that maps every div/button/input to your actual design system components — or Claude Code builds feat…
author: Chris Harper
content:
**Before Claude Code starts adding features, run one substitution pass that replaces Claude Design's generic HTML with your actual design system components — otherwise Claude Code builds around the generics and you pay to fix them later.**

**What you'll be able to do after this:** Run a single pre-handoff prompt that maps every generic HTML element to the closest component in your library, before any feature code accumulates.

Claude Design generates valid, styled markup, but it doesn't know your component library. Its output uses `<div class="card">`, `<button class="btn-primary">`, `<input placeholder="Search">`. Your codebase has `<Card>`, `<Button variant="primary">`, `<SearchInput>`. If you hand that file directly to Claude Code and ask it to add feature logic, it writes the feature around the generic elements. Refactoring later costs a full re-review of everything Claude Code touched ([From Prompt to Production — Design Systems Collective](https://www.designsystemscollective.com/from-prompt-to-production-a-designers-step-by-step-workflow-with-claude-design-claude-code-a7705daad026)).

**The substitution prompt — paste this into a Claude Code session after staging the generated file:**

```
Look at [generated-file.tsx]. Compare every div, button, input, anchor,
and paragraph to the components in src/components/. For each element that
maps cleanly to a named component — same role, compatible props — make the
substitution. Preserve all layout classes, spacing, and event stubs exactly.
Do not change behavior. Stop if a mapping is ambiguous; list what you
couldn't map and why.
```

**Three-step walk-through:**

1. **Stage the export.** Copy your Claude Design export into a temporary file at `src/screens/generated-[feature].tsx` — not directly into your component tree.
2. **Run the substitution pass.** Expect 80–90% of elements to map cleanly on a well-maintained component library. Review the ambiguous list manually; "ambiguous" usually means a layout primitive that has no component equivalent, which is correct behavior.
3. **Commit the substituted file.** Now hand it to Claude Code for feature work. Everything Claude Code touches from this point forward is already in your component vocabulary.

**The limit:** The substitution pass handles clear 1:1 analogues. Highly composed layouts — hero sections, complex data grids, multi-level navigation — often contain patterns without a single matching component. The prompt will tell you what it couldn't map; those are the decisions to make manually before proceeding. Don't re-run the substitution pass after feature code accumulates — the ordering matters.

**Pair this with:** the component inventory technique from [this morning's post](/ai-news/2026-09-04-04-claude-design-multi-screen-component-inventory) (keep components consistent across screens) and the project description technique from [today's design post](/ai-news/2026-09-04-07-claude-design-project-description-brand-brief) (seed stylistic consistency upfront). The substitution pass is the bridge between them.

**Sources:** [From Prompt to Production: A Designers Step-by-Step Workflow with Claude Design + Claude Code — Design Systems Collective](https://www.designsystemscollective.com/from-prompt-to-production-a-designers-step-by-step-workflow-with-claude-design-claude-code-a7705daad026) · [Claude Design workflow — The Design Project](https://designproject.io/blog/claude-design-workflow/)

title: Claude Design Reinvents Your Button on Screen Two — Here's How to Stop It
excerpt: When designing multiple screens in Claude Design, extract a component inventory after screen one and paste it as a constraint in subsequent prompts — this keeps choices consistent across regenerati…
author: Chris Harper
content:
**When designing multiple screens in Claude Design, extract a brief component inventory after screen one and paste it as a constraint in your next prompt — that is the one technique that consistently keeps component choices stable across regenerations.**

AI design tools generate fast but forget. Between two prompts, Claude Design can produce the same feature twice with different button heights, different spacing rhythms, and different card styles — each direction internally consistent, but inconsistent with each other. Practitioners working on multi-step flows report that multi-screen continuity requires deliberate prompting rather than following automatically from shared context ([AI in Design Mid-2026 — Techglock](https://techglock.com/blog/ai-in-design-what-actually-ships-in-mid-2026-and-what-still-falls-apart)).

**The pattern:**

After generating screen one, before moving to screen two, write a brief component inventory — the 10–15 specific choices Claude Design just made:

```
COMPONENT INVENTORY (from screen 1 — do not change these):
- Primary button: 44px height, full-width on mobile, label "Continue"
- Card: 16px padding, 8px border-radius, 1px border #E2E8F0
- Heading: 24px / semibold / no letter-spacing
- Input: 40px height, label above, 4px gap
- Section spacing: 24px between sections, 16px within
```

Open your screen two prompt with: "Match the component inventory above exactly. Do not introduce new visual patterns."

**Why this works instead of longer initial prompts:** Each regeneration is a fresh generation with the existing artboard as visual context — not a continuation of state. The inventory is what carries the decisions across. A longer initial prompt helps screen one; it doesn't bind screen two.

**Limit:** The inventory won't stabilize genuinely different layout structures — a data table, a map view, or a dense multi-column grid will pull in new components regardless. Mark those explicitly: "NEW COMPONENT: data table — all other components match inventory above." Claude Design treats only the marked element as novel and holds everything else.

**Sources:** [AI in Design Mid-2026 — Techglock](https://techglock.com/blog/ai-in-design-what-actually-ships-in-mid-2026-and-what-still-falls-apart) · [Claude Design guides — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com)

title: Is Your System Prompt Actually Being Cached? `/cost` Now Shows the Hit Ratio
excerpt: The /cost command in Claude Code now shows a per-session cache line — hit ratio, misses, and warm vs cold token counts — so you can verify in real time whether your system prompt is landing in cache.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**The `/cost` command in Claude Code now shows a per-session cache line — hit ratio, misses, and warm vs cold token counts — the first direct way to verify in real time whether your system prompt is landing in cache or being re-sent on every turn.**

Running `/cost` in a Claude Code session now returns a line like:

```
Cache: 52% hit ratio · 2 misses · 38k tokens re-cached (warm 34k / cold 4k)
```

Before this, the only signal that your cache was being invalidated was an unexpectedly large bill. Now you can see it per session.

**What the numbers mean:**

- **Hit ratio below 80%:** the cache is being invalidated between turns. Common causes: an MCP server whose tool definitions change on each connection, a hook that writes a timestamp into the system prompt, or (now fixed in recent builds) OAuth token refreshes that cleared the entire prefix hourly.
- **Cold tokens:** charged at full input rates. On Sonnet 5, $2/MTok.
- **Warm tokens:** served from cache. On Sonnet 5, $0.20/MTok — one-tenth the price.

**Tuning cache lifetime with `promptCacheTtl`:**

If your sessions run longer than the default 5-minute cache window, a new setting extends it:

```json
// .claude/settings.json
{
  "promptCacheTtl": 3600,
  "subagentPromptCacheTtl": 300
}
```

`subagentPromptCacheTtl` is separate — useful when you run many short-lived subagents sharing the same context. A shorter value there (e.g. 300s) reduces the cost of re-warming on each agent call.

**Limit:** `promptCacheTtl` only extends the window; it does not prevent invalidation. If content inside the cache prefix is changing between turns — tool definitions, system prompt content, MCP server output — a longer TTL won't help. Diagnose with `/cost` first: if the hit ratio is low, find and stabilize what's changing before adjusting the TTL.

**Sources:** [Claude Code changelog — code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog) · [Prompt caching — Anthropic docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Claude Code context management — claudefa.st](https://claudefa.st/blog/guide/mechanics/context-management)

content:
**Anthropic has made Claude Sonnet 5's $2/$10 per MTok launch pricing permanent — the scheduled September 1 increase to $3/$15 per million input/output tokens will not occur, per the [official pricing docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing).**

Run a sample through both models before assuming Sonnet 5 is cheaper for your specific workload.

title: Your Pipeline Already Speaks OpenAI — Point It at Fireworks AI to Run 250+ Open Models in One Swap
excerpt: Fireworks AI exposes 250+ open-weight models behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint — change one URL and one model string, the rest of your pipeline stays the same.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Fireworks AI exposes 250+ open-weight models (Llama 4, Qwen 3.7, DeepSeek V4) behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint — change one URL and one model string, the rest of your pipeline stays the same.**

**What you'll be able to do after this:** route any prompt through Llama 4, Qwen 3.7, or DeepSeek without rewriting your pipeline, switch models by changing a string, and run cost-sensitive tasks on a model at $0.30/MTok instead of $2/MTok.

**Three things to know first:**
- Fireworks claims its disaggregated prefill/decode architecture reduces latency on large models — per Fireworks' own benchmarks; verify with your specific payload before committing production traffic.
- Free accounts start with a low requests-per-minute ceiling. Adding a payment method raises it, but both per-account and per-model token-per-minute limits apply — plan for rate-limit retries in production.
- The API is compatible with the OpenAI Python SDK and, via `base_url`, with the Anthropic SDK.

**Setup (3 steps):**

1. Get an API key at `fireworks.ai` (free tier works for testing).
2. `pip install openai` if you don't have it.
3. Swap the base URL:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="YOUR_FIREWORKS_KEY",
    base_url="https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="accounts/fireworks/models/llama-4-maverick-instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this PR diff in two sentences."}],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

Model IDs follow the pattern `accounts/fireworks/models/<slug>`. Find the full catalog at `fireworks.ai/models`.

**Limit:** Fireworks' performance figures come from Fireworks itself. There are no published independent benchmarks covering the full 250+ model catalog as of this writing. Measure your p50/p95 on your actual payload before treating their latency numbers as facts. For very short prompts with many concurrent requests, check whether per-model token-per-minute limits become the real bottleneck before blaming latency.

**Sources:** [Fireworks AI inference — fireworks.ai/inference](https://fireworks.ai/inference) · [Fireworks AI API guide — flo2.com](https://flo2.com/blog/fireworks-ai-api-guide) · [Fireworks docs — docs.fireworks.ai](https://docs.fireworks.ai)

title: The Gap Between Claude Design and Your Codebase: When to Regenerate and When to Fix in the Editor
excerpt: Structural drift in a Claude Code implementation goes back to Claude Design. Presentational drift gets fixed in the editor. One rule separates them.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**After Claude Code implements your Claude Design artifact, the result drifts from the spec in two distinct ways. Use one rule to decide: structural problems go back to Claude Design; presentational problems get fixed in the editor.**

Claude Code reads the design artifact — component specs, tokens, layout intent — and generates implementation code. Most of the time it's close. When it isn't, the drift falls into one of two categories.

**Structural drift:** The layout hierarchy is wrong. A sidebar renders inline. A card grid collapses to a single column. A shared sub-component is inlined where it should be extracted. These problems exist because the implementation missed the *structure* of the design intent, not its surface values. **Fix: go back to Claude Design.** Annotate the structural intent more precisely in the artifact (label layout containers, name component boundaries explicitly), then regenerate. Trying to patch structural drift in the editor turns into a long sequence of changes that leaves your code diverged from the design spec — and the next regeneration overwrites them anyway.

**Presentational drift:** The right components are in the right places but values are off. Padding is 16px where the spec says 24px. The primary button renders with the wrong background token. Font weight reads `700` where the design says `600`. **Fix: patch in the editor.** These are implementation errors, not design errors — Claude Code pulled the wrong token or misread a spacing value. Fix them directly and push. Don't round-trip through the design tool for a padding value.

**The practical rule:**
> If you can describe the problem in one sentence containing *where something is* or *what a component is*, go back to the design. If the sentence contains only *what value something has*, fix it in the editor.

**One limit to be aware of:** Claude Design currently regenerates an entire component — there's no way to regenerate just the layout container while preserving the rest. When you go back to fix structural drift, you'll lose any presentational values you've already tuned in the editor. Note them (screenshot or a quick comment) before regenerating, and apply them after. This is the main reason to do structural and presentational fixes in the right order: structure first, presentation last.

**Sources:** [Claude Design — support.claude.com](https://support.claude.com) · [From Prompt to Pull Request: Claude Design + Claude Code — DEV Community](https://dev.to/bilelsalemdev/from-prompt-to-pull-request-using-claude-design-claude-code-and-github-together-3m00) · [Anthropic overhauled Claude Design to fix the handoff — The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/anthropic-claude-design-overhaul/)

title: Sony and Warner Sue Anthropic for Training-Data Scraping — What It Means for AI Product Builders
excerpt: Sony and Warner filed a multi-billion dollar copyright lawsuit against Anthropic on August 29 over training-data scraping. What it means for engineers building on Claude.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell filed a multi-billion dollar copyright lawsuit against Anthropic on August 29, alleging Claude was trained on unlicensed song lyrics scraped at scale. Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann are named personally.**

The complaint, filed in Northern California federal court, accuses Anthropic of "torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale" — naming tens of thousands of song compositions. The publishers seek up to $150,000 per infringed work plus $25,000 per copyright management information violation, yielding potential multi-billion dollar exposure. Anthropic says it will defend itself.

**Three things this does and doesn't mean for engineers building on Claude:**

1. **Downstream liability doesn't automatically flow to API users.** If Anthropic's training data is found infringing, the exposure is Anthropic's, not the product builder's — you're using a deployed model via API, not replicating the training run. The downstream question for API customers remains unsettled in case law; there's no clear precedent yet.

2. **This is the third major music suit against an AI lab** — following earlier cases against Google and Meta. A win for the publishers would force industry-wide reckoning with training data provenance, affecting every major foundation model.

3. **Claude's API and capabilities are unaffected.** Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, and the Claude API remain in production. The suit challenges training methodology, not inference behavior.

**What it doesn't mean:** "Unsafe to build on." IP litigation over training data is structurally separate from model safety or operational risk. Monitor the case alongside the Google and Meta precedents — the outcomes will define what responsible AI training means in law, not just in policy.

**Why it matters:** The legal framework for AI training data is being written in real time. The combined multi-billion dollar exposure, if liability is found, would reshape how every AI lab approaches training data sourcing and licensing.

**Sources:** [Sony, Warner sue Anthropic — TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/08/29/sony-music-warner-sue-anthropic-alleging-a-brazen-campaign-of-intellectual-property-theft/) · [Sony, Warner sue Anthropic — Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/08/29/anthropic-sony-warner-music-copyright) · [Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell sue Anthropic — Music Business Worldwide](https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/now-sony-music-publishing-and-warner-chappell-sue-anthropic-in-multi-billion-dollar-lawsuit-one-of-the-largest-and-most-blatant-ongoing-thefts-of-intellectual-property-in-history/)

title: You're Already on Postgres — Add Vector Search in Five SQL Lines With pgvector
excerpt: pgvector adds a vector column type and similarity search operators to PostgreSQL — add vector search to your existing database with one extension, no new infra.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**pgvector turns your existing PostgreSQL database into a vector store with one extension — no separate service, no new infra. Here's the minimal path from embeddings to similarity search for RAG.**

**What you'll be able to do after this:**
- Add a `vector` column to any Postgres table and store embeddings alongside relational data
- Run cosine similarity search in SQL with two lines
- Add an HNSW index so queries stay fast at 100k+ rows

## Enable the extension

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
```

On Supabase: one toggle in Database → Extensions. On AWS RDS (PostgreSQL 15+) or Azure Database for PostgreSQL: enable from the extensions list. For a local Postgres install: `apt install postgresql-16-pgvector`, then run the SQL above.

## Store embeddings

```sql
CREATE TABLE documents (
  id        SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  content   TEXT,
  embedding VECTOR(1536)  -- match your model's output dimension
);
```

From Python, generate embeddings with `sentence-transformers` or any embedding endpoint and insert with `psycopg2`:

```python
import psycopg2
cur.execute(
    "INSERT INTO documents (content, embedding) VALUES (%s, %s)",
    (chunk_text, embedding_list)
)
```

## Query by similarity

```sql
SELECT content, 1 - (embedding <=> %s::vector) AS score
FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding <=> %s::vector
LIMIT 5;
```

`<=>` is cosine distance; `<->` is L2 (Euclidean); `<#>` is negative inner product. For normalized embeddings, all three produce the same ranking — cosine (`<=>`) is the safe default.

## Add an index before production

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);
```

Without an index, pgvector does a full table scan — fine under ~10k rows, noticeable past that. HNSW keeps query time in low milliseconds at 100k+ rows.

## When to use something else

pgvector uses Postgres CPU and I/O budget. If you're storing millions of vectors with heavy concurrent load, a dedicated vector database (Qdrant, Chroma, Pinecone) offloads the index pressure and keeps your Postgres instance uncontested. For a typical RAG app under ~500k documents, staying in Postgres means one fewer service to run, one fewer connection to manage, and free joins against your existing tables.

**The best starting resource:** [pgvector: Embeddings and vector similarity — Supabase Docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/extensions/pgvector) covers setup, LangChain integration, and metadata filtering. For a hands-on video: [PGVector: Turn PostgreSQL into Vector Database (Python Tutorial) — YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=erNoI9COOn0).

**Sources:** [pgvector extension — Supabase Docs](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/extensions/pgvector) · [pgvector tutorial — DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/tutorial/pgvector-tutorial) · [You probably don't need a vector database — Encore](https://encore.dev/blog/you-probably-dont-need-a-vector-database)

title: Your Component Needs a Bigger Change: Step Back Into Claude Design Before Touching Code
excerpt: When an existing component needs a layout shift or structural rework, run /design with the current code as context to explore directions before any file changes are committed.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**When an existing component needs more than a style tweak — a layout shift, a structural rework — run `/design` with the current code as context to explore directions before any file changes are committed.**

The default Claude Design flow is linear: sketch → implement. The reverse loop — code → design — is what you reach for when a component already exists and the problem isn't a CSS property but a structural one.

**The workflow:**

1. In your Claude Code session, run `/design explore directions for [component name]` and paste the component's current JSX or reference its file path. Claude Code reads your DESIGN.md and existing design system context, then drafts 2–3 artboard directions in the `/design` preview. It already knows your tokens, components, and layout conventions from earlier file reads.

2. Review the directions in the artboard. You can click elements to adjust colors, spacing, or text directly before committing — this is where you catch "this feels wrong" before code changes are in flight.

3. Pick the direction and tell Claude to implement it. It writes to the actual component file starting from the artboard structure, not as an incremental patch on the old layout.

**When to use this vs. just editing:** Use the design loop when the fix requires rethinking where elements sit — layout, hierarchy, visual weight. If the fix is "change this color to match the token" or "fix the margin", just edit. The fork is worth the extra step only when you genuinely don't know which direction is right.

**The limit:** the artboard preview renders a static snapshot — it doesn't pull live component state (loading skeletons, error states, empty states). If those matter for your redesign, spec them explicitly in your `/design` prompt or in DESIGN.md before you implement. Edge states you don't name tend to come out as empty-div placeholders that pass a quick visual check and break in production.

**Sources:** [Claude Code /design — What's New Week 34, code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/whats-new/2026-w34) · [Claude Design + Claude Code Workflow 2026 — vanbeaumond.nl](https://vanbeaumond.nl/en/blog/claude-design-claude-code-workflow-setup-2026) · [Claude Design to Claude Code: AI Design Handoff — claudefa.st](https://claudefa.st/blog/guide/mechanics/claude-design-handoff)

title: Fork a Running Session to Explore a Risky Approach Without Losing Your Place
excerpt: Run /fork to copy your entire conversation into a background session that runs independently — full history, context, and model settings inherited — while your original keeps going.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**`/fork` copies your entire conversation — history, context, model settings — into a background session that runs independently while your original keeps going.**

When you're deep in a Claude Code session and realize you want to try something that might not work — a big refactor, an architectural change, a destructive migration — there's a fork.

Run `/fork [description]` and Claude Code creates a new background session with an identical copy of your conversation: the same history, system prompt, tool definitions, and model settings. Your original session keeps going. The fork appears in `claude agents` with its own labeled row.

**Why fork beats a clean subagent for exploratory work:** a clean subagent starts fresh and needs briefing. A fork inherits everything the session already knows — the codebase context you've built up, the discussion about which approach to take, the files you've already read. For exploratory work on a complex codebase, that inheritance is the difference between a useful branch and a wasted re-briefing.

```bash
# Branch off the current session to try a risky migration approach
/fork "explore multi-tenant DB migration with separate schemas"

# Your original session keeps responding to your next prompt
# Check the fork's progress anytime
claude agents
```

**Limit:** the fork can't write back to the parent session's state. Its file changes land in your working tree like any other subagent's. If the approach works, you review and merge the branch. If it doesn't, you abandon the fork — your original session is untouched.

`subagent_type: "fork"` in a skill or agent definition does the same thing programmatically when you want inherited context for a specific delegated task rather than a clean-slate subagent.

**Sources:** [Claude Code sub-agents — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) · [Fork vs. subagent in Claude Code — DEV Community](https://dev.to/rulestack/claude-code-fork-vs-subagent-what-fork-subtask-and-subagenttype-fork-each-copy-229a) · [Forked Subagents in Claude Code — mejba.me](https://www.mejba.me/blog/forked-subagents-claude-code-anthropic)

title: Google Ships Gemini 3.8 Flash at $0.75/MTok with Upgraded Coding Performance
excerpt: Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2 at $0.75/$3.75 per million tokens — a coding-focused Flash-tier model available via the Gemini API and AI Studio.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash on September 2, a coding-focused Flash-tier model at $0.75/$3.75 per million tokens — worth adding to your benchmark set before routing inference to it.**

Google shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash (internally "Skimaki") on September 2, 2026. It's available via the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and consumer Gemini surfaces, priced at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output.

Google reports internal testing in their Jetski developer platform preferred this model over Claude Opus for coding tasks — that is Google's own benchmark, not an independent evaluation, and no third-party coding benchmark results were published at launch.

Two things to verify before routing workloads to it: the knowledge cutoff varies by domain (March 2026 for some areas, January 2025 for others), which matters for tasks involving recent APIs or events. Google also shipped Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber alongside the general model, replacing the 3.5 Cyber variant for security-focused workloads.

**Why it matters:** Another Flash-tier option at a price point below Sonnet-tier for longer coding runs. Run your own evals on your actual workload — Flash-tier models vary substantially by task type, and internal benchmark results from any lab rarely translate directly to production.

title: See Every Subagent Tool Call From Your Phone — and Know If Your Cache Is Working: Claude Code v2.1.251
excerpt: Claude Code v2.1.251 streams foreground subagent tool calls live to Remote Control clients, and /cost now shows per-session cache hit ratio. Two signals for monitoring long agentic runs from anywhere.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Claude Code v2.1.251 (August 28) streams foreground subagent tool calls live to Remote Control clients, and `/cost` now shows per-session cache hit ratio, misses, and re-cached tokens — the two signals you need to monitor a long agentic run from anywhere.**

**Foreground subagent live streaming.** When a subagent runs in the foreground, its tool calls and results — file reads, bash executions, writes — now stream in real time to connected Remote Control clients (phone or desktop companion). Background subagents (the default) still show status only.

This gives you per-step visibility on a running multi-agent session without staying at the terminal. It's most useful for tasks where you want to be able to interrupt mid-operation: security-sensitive file changes, anything involving credentials, or workflows where a bad tool call deep in the chain would be expensive to roll back.

**Cache visibility in `/cost`.** A new `prompt_cache` line shows: hit ratio, misses, tokens re-cached from the last run, and whether the cache is warm or cold for this session. If you're relying on prompt caching to keep session costs down and haven't been able to confirm it's working, this is the output that tells you.

```
/cost now includes:
  Cache:  82% hit ratio · 4.2K misses · 38K tokens re-cached · warm
```

Also new: a spend limit bar in `/usage` and a `rate_limits.spend_limit` field for status line scripts, for environments behind a Claude apps gateway with a monthly spend ceiling.

**When to use foreground vs. background subagents.** Foreground streaming is best when you need per-step accountability — security-sensitive operations, anything involving credentials, or workflows where you want to be able to interrupt cleanly. Background subagents remain the right default for parallelized, fire-and-forget work (batch analysis, test runs, research pipelines).

**Real limit.** Foreground subagent streaming relays through the Remote Control service — each tool call result waits for that relay. On tight agentic loops this adds measurable latency. Don't switch to foreground just for visibility unless you actually need per-step control; the overhead is real, not just theoretical.

**Sources:** [Claude Code v2.1.251 release — github.com/anthropics/claude-code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/releases/tag/v2.1.251) · [Claude Code v2.1.250 to v2.1.251 key updates — dev.classmethod.jp](https://dev.classmethod.jp/en/articles/20260829-cc-updates-v2-1-251/) · [Claude Code sub-agents — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents)

title: OpenAI's Astra Is the First AI Model Rated "Critical" for Cybersecurity — It Found Zero-Days on Its Own

author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: OpenAI's Astra is the first model rated "Critical" under its Preparedness Framework — it autonomously found zero-day vulnerabilities and built working browser-escape and OS privilege-escalation chains during evaluations.**

In expert-led assessments, Astra scored 100% on ExploitBench (which measures exploit-chain generation from known CVEs), discovered two previously unknown zero-days during separate evaluations on recently disclosed flaws, built a full browser-compromise chain that escaped a sandbox and executed host OS commands, and chained multiple hardened-OS vulnerabilities into a privilege-escalation path.

OpenAI reports the model declines 91.5% of cyber-related jailbreak attempts — up from 59% for GPT-5.6 Sol. That still means roughly 1 in 11 targeted attempts succeeds, which is a real failure rate for security-sensitive deployments.

The "Critical" designation means Astra will be released, not blocked, but with gated access through OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program for vetted security researchers — the same capability-gated access pattern Anthropic applied last month for Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.

**Why it matters:** Autonomous exploit-chain discovery — no per-step human guidance — changes the threat model for agentic systems with broad tool access to shell, file system, or network. If you're building agents with those permissions, ExploitBench capability rating is now the reference point for what adversarial misuse looks like.

title: Your Retriever Returns 10 Chunks. Your LLM Needs One. Contextual Compression Fixes the Gap.
excerpt: LangChain's ContextualCompressionRetriever wraps any retriever and strips irrelevant content from retrieved chunks before the LLM call. Two compressor options: EmbeddingsFilter (fast) or LLMChainEx…
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: LangChain's `ContextualCompressionRetriever` wraps your existing retriever and strips irrelevant content from retrieved chunks before they reach the LLM — no architecture change, two compressor options.**

**What you'll be able to do after this:** Add a compression layer that either drops low-relevance chunks entirely (EmbeddingsFilter, no extra LLM call) or extracts only the relevant sentences from each chunk (LLMChainExtractor, one cheap LLM call per chunk).

**Three things to know:**
1. **EmbeddingsFilter** is the fast path: embed the query and each chunk, drop anything below a cosine similarity threshold (`0.76` is a reasonable starting value). No LLM call, sub-millisecond overhead per chunk.
2. **LLMChainExtractor** is the quality path: send each chunk to the LLM and ask it to extract only what's relevant to the query. Adds one call per chunk but can compress a 2,000-token chunk to 80 tokens when most of it is noise.
3. **DocumentCompressorPipeline** chains them: filter first (EmbeddingsFilter removes irrelevant chunks cheaply), then extract (LLMChainExtractor compresses the survivors). Best of both at the cost of both.

**Walk-through — EmbeddingsFilter (fast, cheap):**

```python
from langchain.retrievers import ContextualCompressionRetriever
from langchain.retrievers.document_compressors import EmbeddingsFilter
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings

# Your existing retriever — Chroma, FAISS, pgvector, etc.
base_retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 10})

embeddings_filter = EmbeddingsFilter(
    embeddings=OpenAIEmbeddings(),
    similarity_threshold=0.76  # tune per corpus: lower = more permissive
)
compression_retriever = ContextualCompressionRetriever(
    base_compressor=embeddings_filter,
    base_retriever=base_retriever
)

docs = compression_retriever.invoke("What are the failure modes of RAG pipelines?")
# Typically returns 2-4 chunks instead of 10
```

**Walk-through — LLMChainExtractor (highest quality):**

```python
from langchain.retrievers.document_compressors import LLMChainExtractor
from langchain_anthropic import ChatAnthropic

extractor = LLMChainExtractor.from_llm(
    ChatAnthropic(model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001")  # cheap model works fine here
)
compression_retriever = ContextualCompressionRetriever(
    base_compressor=extractor,
    base_retriever=base_retriever
)
```

Drop-in replacement: use `compression_retriever` anywhere you'd use `base_retriever`.

**Real limits.** `similarity_threshold` needs per-corpus tuning — a value that works on one dataset may over-filter on another, silently dropping relevant chunks. `LLMChainExtractor` adds one LLM call *per retrieved chunk*: at `k=10`, that's 10 extra calls before the main generation; on high-traffic systems this doubles both latency and cost. Neither technique fixes a bad retriever — if your vector search returns the wrong documents, compression gives you a smaller wrong set.

**Sources:** [LangChain contextual compression how-to](https://python.langchain.com/docs/how_to/contextual_compression/) · [NirDiamant RAG_Techniques: contextual_compression.ipynb](https://github.com/NirDiamant/RAG_Techniques/blob/main/all_rag_techniques/contextual_compression.ipynb) · [LangChain OpenTutorial: ContextualCompressionRetriever](https://langchain-opentutorial.gitbook.io/langchain-opentutorial/10-retriever/02-contextualcompressionretriever)

title: Put a Cost Ceiling on Every Subagent in Your Workflow: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE
excerpt: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 pins every subagent, teammate, and workflow agent in your Claude Code session to one model — overriding per-definition settings. Two env vars, one settings.json e…
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=haiku` and `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` to cap every subagent, teammate, and workflow agent in your session to one model — even if their definitions request Opus. New in v2.1.257.**

When you fan out work across 10 subagents, each one inherits your main session's model by default. If that's Opus 5, a 10-agent workflow burns 10 times the context at Opus rates. Two environment variables give you a ceiling.

**What each variable does:**

- `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` sets the fallback model for subagents when nothing else specifies one — but it does NOT override agent definition frontmatter or the built-in Explore and Plan agents.
- `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` overrides everything: per-invocation model parameters, agent definition frontmatter, and the built-in Explore and Plan agents.

**Add both to `.claude/settings.json` for project-wide enforcement:**

```json
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL": "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
    "CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE": "1"
  }
}
```

Or set per-session in your shell:

```bash
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=sonnet
export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1
claude
```

**Model resolution order without FORCE:** per-invocation `model` param → agent definition frontmatter → `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` → main session model.

**With FORCE=1:** `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` wins for everything above — except forks and skills with `model: inherit`, which still run on the main conversation's model by design (you don't control the skills you didn't write).

**Real limits.** Forcing Explore and Plan to Haiku degrades their quality on complex research tasks — those built-in agents are tuned for thoroughness. If your workflow's search or planning quality drops, set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` to Sonnet instead, or remove FORCE and pin specific agent definitions individually via their frontmatter. The env var covers the entire session; there's no per-workflow override within a single session.

**Sources:** [Claude Code v2.1.257 changelog — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog#2-1-257) · [Sub-agent model configuration — code.claude.com](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents) · [Claude Code Subagents: A 2026 Practical Guide — Tembo.io](https://www.tembo.io/blog/claude-code-subagents)

title: Your RAG Pipeline Returns Answers. Here's How to Tell If They're True: Ragas in 10 Lines
excerpt: Ragas scores any RAG pipeline's hallucination rate, answer relevancy, and retrieval quality using LLM-as-judge — four metrics, one evaluate() call, each localizing a different failure mode.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Ragas adds four LLM-as-judge metrics to any RAG pipeline — faithfulness, answer relevancy, context precision, and context recall — so you can measure where it hallucinates and which stage to fix.**

**What you'll be able to do after this:** score a RAG pipeline's accuracy, relevance, and retrieval quality programmatically, so you know whether a change helped or hurt before it reaches users.

**Three things to take away:**

- **Faithfulness catches hallucinations.** Ragas extracts claims from the answer and checks each against the retrieved chunks. If an answer claims something the chunks don't support, faithfulness drops below 1.0.
- **Context precision catches retrieval ordering failures.** It scores whether the chunks that actually helped generate the answer were ranked near the top of what was retrieved — poor ranking wastes your context window on irrelevant content.
- **LLM-as-judge costs real tokens.** Each metric makes several LLM calls per sample. Batch your evaluation set and run it on a random sample of production queries, not a hand-picked "good" set, or the scores tell you nothing.

**Install and run a basic evaluation:**

```bash
pip install ragas openai datasets
```

```python
from datasets import Dataset
from ragas import evaluate
from ragas.metrics import faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision

data = {
    "question": ["What is chunking in RAG?"],
    "answer": ["Chunking splits documents into segments that match the embedding model's token limit."],
    "contexts": [["Document chunking divides text into segments sized to fit the embedding model."]],
    # "ground_truth": ["..."]  # only needed for context_recall
}
dataset = Dataset.from_dict(data)

result = evaluate(dataset, metrics=[faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision])
print(result)
# {'faithfulness': 1.0, 'answer_relevancy': 0.91, 'context_precision': 0.88}
```

**How to read the scores.** Low faithfulness (< 0.8): your model is adding facts the retrieved chunks don't contain — tighten your prompt or fix chunking. Low context precision: useful chunks are buried in retrieval results — check your embedding model or similarity threshold. Low answer relevancy: the answer is drifting from the question — revisit your generation prompt.

**Best starting video:** [RAG Evaluation Matrix — RAGAS Metrics: Faithfulness, Context Precision, Recall](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZqrprZWfsg) walks through all four metrics with code (April 2026).

**Real limits.** Faithfulness only checks consistency with retrieved context, not world-truth: a pipeline can score 1.0 faithfulness while still being factually wrong if the retrieved chunks themselves contain errors. `context_recall` requires ground-truth reference answers — without labeled data, skip it. LLM-as-judge scores carry the judge model's biases toward longer, more fluent outputs and toward its own family's style. Ragas is a floor, not a ceiling: 1.0 faithfulness means you passed, not that the answers are correct.

**Sources:** [Ragas documentation — docs.ragas.io](https://docs.ragas.io) · [Evaluation of RAG pipelines with Ragas — Langfuse](https://langfuse.com/guides/cookbook/evaluation_of_rag_with_ragas) · [Evaluate RAG with Ragas + watsonx — IBM](https://www.ibm.com/think/tutorials/evaluate-rag-pipeline-using-ragas-in-python-with-watsonx)

title: Anthropic Adds Customer-Controlled Storage for Frontier Model API Traffic
excerpt: Enterprise Frontier Safeguards store Claude Fable 5/5.1 API traffic in your own S3/Azure/GCS bucket — customer encryption keys, no Anthropic human review. Phased rollout this fall.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Anthropic's Enterprise Frontier Safeguards store Fable 5/5.1 API traffic in your own S3/Azure/GCS bucket — customer encryption keys, automated misuse detection, no Anthropic human review.**

Anthropic introduced a 30-day data retention requirement with Fable 5 in June, citing the need to detect sophisticated misuse patterns that span multiple sessions and accounts. Enterprise customers with data-sovereignty requirements pushed back. EFS is the fix: interaction data stays in infrastructure you control. Anthropic's pattern-detection runs against your storage and returns only category-level signals — not the underlying prompts.

Three practical facts:
- Anthropic doesn't charge for EFS; your cloud provider bills storage and data operations at standard rates.
- Works whether you access Claude directly or through AWS Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, or GCP Vertex.
- Phased rollout through fall 2026; eligible customers receive zero retention on Fable 5/5.1 as an interim measure now.

**Limit to note:** customer-controlled storage is not the same as zero retention — data still exists, in your cloud account. Fully automated review also means Anthropic cannot assist with incident reconstruction that would require content review.

**Why it matters:** If a data-residency or compliance requirement has been blocking your team from Fable 5 or 5.1, EFS is the unlock — customer-owned storage satisfies most data-sovereignty policies without losing the frontier model tier.

title: Your Fine-Tune Has No Data Yet. Here's How to Build the Dataset Without Annotators.
excerpt: HuggingFace's Synthetic Data Generator builds chat-format JSONL datasets from a task description and seed examples — LLM generates, LLM judges, push to Hub, load in SFTTrainer.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Generate a JSONL fine-tuning dataset without annotators — describe your task, seed it with examples, HuggingFace's Synthetic Data Generator drafts and LLM-judges them, then push straight to the Hub.**

**What you'll be able to do after this:** Generate a chat-format fine-tuning dataset from a task description and five seed examples, filter it with an LLM judge, push the result to HuggingFace Hub, and load it into TRL's SFTTrainer in a single `datasets.load_dataset()` call.

**Three key ideas:**
- **LLM as teacher.** A frontier model (default: Llama 3.3 70B via the free HuggingFace Inference API) generates diverse variations of your seed examples. The seed shapes the style; the LLM fills the volume.
- **LLM as judge.** A second pass scores each generated example for quality and task alignment. Low-scoring examples are filtered before the dataset is pushed. The 2026 finding from synthetic-data research: an unfiltered dataset is reliably worse than a smaller filtered one.
- **JSONL chat format.** Each entry is `{"messages": [{"role": "system", ...}, {"role": "user", ...}, {"role": "assistant", ...}]}` — the same format TRL's SFTTrainer and Unsloth's FastLanguageModel both consume directly.

**Walk-through:**
1. Open the [Synthetic Data Generator Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/argilla/synthetic-data-generator) — free, no GPU required.
2. Describe your dataset in plain language: "customer support chat for a Python SDK, questions about rate limits and auth errors."
3. Add 3–5 seed examples to anchor the style and vocabulary.
4. Select **Chat Dataset**, set sample count (200 is enough to verify quality), click Generate.
5. Review a sample in the Argilla panel; re-generate any section that's off.
6. Push to Hub → `datasets.load_dataset("your-org/dataset-name")` in your training script.

**Limits:** The Spaces version only handles text classification and chat datasets; RAG, preference, and eval tasks require the distilabel Python SDK directly. Generation speed is ~20 samples/minute on the free Inference API — budget an hour for 1,000 examples. Quality is bounded by your seed: vague seeds produce coherent but useless data. Switch to a local or paid inference endpoint for larger volumes.

**Sources:** [Introducing the Synthetic Data Generator — HuggingFace Blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/synthetic-data-generator) · [Synthetic Data for LLM Fine-Tuning in 2026 — Future AGI](https://futureagi.com/blog/synthetic-data-fine-tuning-llms/) · [distilabel docs — Argilla/HuggingFace](https://distilabel.argilla.io)

title: Fable 5.1 Ships Today: Cache Reads Drop From $1.00 to $0.25 per Million Tokens
excerpt: Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 today. Cache reads drop to $0.25/M — 75% cheaper, cutting agentic workload costs 25-45%, per Anthropic.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Anthropic launched Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 today (September 1). Cache reads drop from $1.00 to $0.25 per million tokens — Anthropic reports this cuts effective costs 25% on typical workloads and up to 45% on heavily agentic ones.**

Cache reads are the compounding cost in agentic systems: every time an agent revisits the same system prompt, tool definitions, or accumulated context, it triggers a read. Fable 5's $1.00/M rate made this expensive for long-running Claude Code sessions and multi-step pipelines. At $0.25/M, the same re-use is 75% cheaper. Cache write prices are unchanged ($12.50/M for 5-min, $20/M for 1-hr); the savings are entirely on reads.

Input and output prices are unchanged at $10/$50 per million tokens. The model outperforms Fable 5 on Anthropic's internal evals, with the biggest gains in computer use, long-horizon agentic work, and terminal-based engineering tasks. Knowledge cutoff is June 2026. Fable 5.1's cybersecurity capabilities are strong enough that some queries in that domain are automatically rerouted to Opus models — test any security tooling built on the API before assuming behavior is identical to Fable 5.

**Mythos 5.1** ships alongside with restricted access to vetted US organizations (cyberdefenders and life scientists only, via a separate application process). Not broadly available.

**What to do today**

If you've enabled prompt caching in your pipeline (via the `cache_control` parameter), update your model string to the Fable 5.1 identifier (see the [Anthropic announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-1) for the exact string). No other code changes needed — the 75% read savings apply automatically to any already-cached context.

**Limits:**
- The 25–45% effective cost reduction is Anthropic's own estimate; independent controlled comparisons don't exist yet. Treat it as directionally correct.
- At $10/$50/M input/output, Fable 5.1 remains the most expensive tier in the Anthropic lineup. Cache savings help pipelines with heavy context re-use; fresh-context requests see no change.
- Knowledge cutoff June 2026 means it has no awareness of events from the past three months.

**Why it matters:** Agentic pipelines that re-use context pay 75% less per cache read starting today — update the model string and the savings apply automatically.

**Sources:** [Introducing Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 — Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-1) · [System Card, Sep 1 2026 — Anthropic](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/0339e6a7c5c7b87f5c07798616dc32c215d14235/Claude%20Fable%205.1%20%26%20Claude%20Mythos%205.1%20System%20Card.pdf) · [Cache reads 75% cheaper — VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/technology/anthropics-claude-fable-5-1-and-mythos-5-1-arrive-with-a-75-cost-reduction-for-fable-cache-reads) · [Fable 5.1: cheaper, smarter, refuses less — The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/anthropic-fable-5-1-launch/)

title: Run Any Open-Source Model With Two Lines of Code: Together AI's OpenAI-Compatible Inference API
excerpt: Together AI wraps 200+ open models behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint — swap one URL and one model string to run Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek R1, or Qwen 2.5 without managing GPU infrastructure.
author: Chris Harper
content:
**TL;DR: Together AI's inference API is an OpenAI-compatible endpoint for 200+ open models — two lines of code to switch from any closed-model API to Llama, DeepSeek, or Qwen without touching the rest of your pipeline.**

**What you'll be able to do after this:**
- Replace closed-model calls with open-weight inference without rewriting your SDK code
- Run Llama 3.3 70B, DeepSeek R1, and Qwen 2.5 on managed infrastructure at open-model pricing
- Deploy fine-tuned LoRA adapters to serverless inference using the same endpoint

[Resource: Together AI inference quickstart](https://docs.together.ai/docs/quickstart) · [Sentdex Together API Basics notebook (GitHub)](https://github.com/Sentdex/Together-API-Basics/blob/main/together-api-examples.ipynb)

**The two-line swap**

If your code uses the OpenAI Python SDK, switching to Together AI is a URL and API key change:

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.together.xyz/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["TOGETHER_API_KEY"],
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Classify this support ticket: ..."}],
    max_tokens=512,
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

The same `tools=`, `response_format=`, and streaming patterns work identically — Together's API surface matches OpenAI's completion spec.

**Model naming**

Together uses `<provider>/<model-id>` format. Key models as of September 2026:

- Llama 3.3 70B Instruct: `meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo`
- DeepSeek R1: `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1`
- Qwen 2.5 72B: `Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct-Turbo`
- Mistral 7B: `mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3`

Browse the full catalog at [api.together.xyz/models](https://api.together.xyz/models).

**Streaming**

```python
stream = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-Turbo",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain reranking in three sentences."}],
    stream=True,
)
for chunk in stream:
    print(chunk.choices[0].delta.content or "", end="", flush=True)
```

**Deploying a fine-tuned adapter**

Together's native fine-tuning lets you train a LoRA adapter on the platform and serve it at the same per-token rate as the base model — no additional hosting cost per adapter slot. Once training completes, your custom model ID appears in the catalog and you call it identically to any base model. If you've trained an adapter with Unsloth or HuggingFace TRL, Together is a direct path from adapter weights to a serverless endpoint without managing vLLM infrastructure yourself.

**Together vs OpenRouter: when to use which**

Together AI is a single provider with its own GPU infrastructure. OpenRouter is a routing proxy across 70+ providers. Use OpenRouter to compare models during development (one string change switches the model); migrate to Together when you've committed to a specific open model and want the lowest per-token rate and no routing overhead. Together wins when you also need native fine-tuning — OpenRouter doesn't handle adapters.

**Real limits**

- Together's catalog (200+ models) is smaller than OpenRouter's 400+. Check [api.together.xyz/models](https://api.together.xyz/models) before assuming your model is available.
- No automatic provider fallback. If Together has an outage, your retry logic is your responsibility — OpenRouter handles this for you.
- The free tier allows limited daily calls; production traffic requires API credits. Per Together's pricing pages, serverless rates vary by model — verify current prices before building cost estimates.
- Together claims top time-to-first-token on many open models; independent latency comparisons shift as providers upgrade hardware. Measure in your own region and context window size before depending on published rankings.
